subject: Post-demo: Acme perf constraints, streaming needs & cost levers

Subject: Post-demo: Acme perf constraints, streaming needs & cost levers

Hi Dana —

Thanks again for the demo slot today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum. I focused this note on the performance/qualification items you asked us to confirm after the call.

Key perf targets you mentioned (please confirm if I captured correctly):
- P95 latency target: <= 150 ms for prompt+512 token generation (token-level streaming to client)
- Sustained throughput: ~80 QPS for single-region traffic (US)
- Concurrent sessions: 40–60 simultaneous user sessions with KV cache reuse per user
- Max tail requirement: 99.9th percentile must be within 2x P95 for spikes

Streaming/UX constraints: low start-of-response time (first token < 50 ms preferred) and incremental tokens every ~20–40 ms once streaming begins.

Cost sensitivity: you mentioned a desire to stay within a per-1000-token budget that’s competitive vs your current provider — we’ll propose levers to hit both latency and cost targets.

Immediate next steps I propose:
1) Confirmation of the perf targets above (reply with edits).
2) Marcus to run a quick micro-benchmark mapping our model variants to the latency/throughput targets for your median input size.
3) Hannah to prepare a short cost/runbook showing tradeoffs (continuous batching, prefix caching, quantized model variants).
4) Share an SLO matrix and demo recording (attached).

Attachments: acme_slo_matrix.xlsx (initial SLO worksheet), redwood_cost_model_v2.pdf (cost levers explainer), demo-recording-20261207.mp4 (recording).

If that plan looks good I’ll schedule a 45-minute follow up next week to review Marcus' micro-benchmark and Hannah's cost scenarios.

Thanks —

Vanessa —

Thanks for the concise recap. Mostly correct; a few clarifications:
- P95: we really want p95 <= 150 ms for median prompt lengths (~120 tokens input, ~256 tokens output). For longer flows (input ~500 tokens), acceptable p95 is up to 250 ms, but p99 must stay < 600 ms.
- Throughput: 80 QPS is peak for a single storefront; weeknight baseline is ~25 QPS.
- Concurrency: 50 active sessions with KV reuse per session is accurate.
- Streaming: First token < 100 ms acceptable; token cadence ~30–50 ms.

Budget note: we have a procurement budget target (TCO) and are sensitive to per-token cost and number of reserved GPU hours. Tom is looping in procurement for any reserved capacity discussion.

Please send Marcus' micro-bench and Hannah's cost scenarios. Also include any proposed fallback policy if a higher-latency event occurs (e.g., degrade to a smaller model variant).

Regards,
Dana
Dana Liu, CTO — Acme Retail
From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
To: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa_ortiz@redwood.ai>, Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 09 Dec 2026 08:12:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Post-demo: Acme perf constraints, streaming needs & cost levers

Vanessa / Hannah —

I ran a focused micro-benchmark overnight against the three candidate model variants we discussed (base-open, distilled-6B, and quantized-6B int8) on a single A100-like instance profile with Redwood's continuous-batching enabled. Quick summary (numbers are median of 10 runs with 256-token outputs and 120-token prompts):
- base-open (full fp16): p50=42ms, p95=168ms, p99=340ms, tokens/sec steady-state=210
- distilled-6B (fp16): p50=34ms, p95=120ms, p99=260ms, tokens/sec=320
- quantized-6B (int8, weight-only quant): p50=38ms, p95=135ms, p99=280ms, tokens/sec=300

Observations and levers to hit your targets:
1) For p95 <=150 ms at 256-token outputs, the distilled-6B meets target comfortably and also gives better throughput (lower cost).
2) Quantized-6B is close to distilled in latency and is a win for cost per token; need to validate quality regression on your eval prompts.
3) Continuous batching with dynamic batch caps (batch size 8–16 depending on tail risk) will reduce per-token cost by ~25% vs single-request serving while preserving p95 for most traffic shapes.
4) Prefix/KV caching: if you can reuse KV cache across sessions (customer-specific session pinning), cold-start costs drop dramatically; effective QPS with caching looks 1.6–2x better.
5) Streaming: to meet the first-token goal (<100 ms), we should enable model-level early-start (generate-first-token pipeline) plus aggressive kernel selection for short prefixes; this trades a small increase in CPU overhead for much lower TTF.

Proposed technical recommendation: run a 2-hour spike test with distilled-6B and quantized-6B under continuous batching + KV caching enabled to validate p95/p99 under synthetic spike patterns (80 QPS peak). If quality drift acceptable for quantized-6B, prefer that for cost.

I can run that tomorrow and dump detailed logs and token-level latencies to the shared Drive link.

-Marcus
Principal Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference

Dana / Tom —

Thanks — Marcus' bench above is attached as an initial findings summary. Key ask from our side: please confirm whether you want us to run the 2-hour spike test in your staging region (we can simulate traffic from US-west) or run in our dedicated sandbox and send results. Staging gives the most realistic network+region latency numbers.

Hannah will follow with an explicit cost/runbook that maps the two recommended deployment options:
A) Production-optimized (distilled-6B, reserved capacity for predictable latency) — higher committed cost, lowest per-token cost and tightest p95. Includes canary rollout and automatic fallback to quantized-6B.
B) Cost-first (quantized-6B with autoscaling, aggressive prefix caching) — lower committed spend, slightly higher p99 tail risk; good if you want conservative reserved hours.

Attachments: acme_slo_matrix.xlsx, redwood_cost_model_v2.pdf, demo-recording-20261207.mp4 (same as earlier).

Proposed next meeting: 45 minutes next Tue 2026-12-15 10:00 PT to review the 2-hour test output + cost tradeoffs. I’ll add a calendar invite once you confirm staging vs sandbox.
